analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall between banks that hold deposits and firms that underwrite securities.
analysis.headline: The bill received no committee action and no cosponsors, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have re-built the old Glass-Steagall separation from the 1930s, which used to forbid banks that take insured deposits from also being part of companies that sell and trade stocks and bonds. It would also bar securities executives from running deposit banks at the same time, and stop banks from selling insurance. The aim was to keep everyday depositors' money away from risky Wall Street dealing, reducing the chance of another bailout. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, got no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor, and expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers. Separating deposit banking from securities underwriting lowers the chance that a bank's risky trading losses threaten the insured deposits of regular customers and force taxpayer rescues. Bank employees who work only in traditional banking also gain from a safer employer.

how_it_helps.text: Forbids a member bank from being affiliated with a company principally engaged in issuing, underwriting, or selling stocks, bonds, or other securities, effective one year after enactment [S2] [S3].
Bars officers, directors, and employees of securities firms from simultaneously serving as officers, directors, or employees of a member bank, with limited Federal Reserve exceptions [S2] [S3].
Prohibits depository institutions from engaging in the business of insurance or any insurance-related activity [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large universal banks that combine commercial banking with securities underwriting and insurance sales would have to break apart or spin off those businesses within a year of enactment. Major Wall Street banks built on the combined model would bear the largest restructuring costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big universal banks and securities firms

drawbacks.text: Reversing the 1999 repeal would force abrupt divestitures: the bill gave banks only one year from enactment to unwind affiliations, a timeline even supporters of separation often called disruptive [S3].

Restoring Glass-Steagall alone would not address the risks that fueled the 2008 crisis, much of which came from unregulated nonbank institutions and derivatives outside the commercial-investment banking divide; a good-faith objection is that the bill addresses a real problem only partially.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea—keeping insured deposits away from securities underwriting—is a genuine protection for depositors and taxpayers, and many economists after the 2008 crash supported some version of it. But this bill was a blunt one-year, full-scale reversal with no transition study, and it would not have covered the shadow-banking risks that actually drove 2008. As drafted it was a signal bill, not a carefully sequenced reform, and it never advanced far enough to be tested in amendments.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or a vote; the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the Banking Integrity Act of 2010 on January 15, 2010 [S1] [S5].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died without coming to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large universal banks and securities firms that would have had to break up their combined banking, securities, and insurance operations kept the status quo, since the bill never even reached a hearing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big combined banks kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it died in committee.

against.name: Rep. Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: As chairman, did not schedule the bill for committee action during the 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows only that the bill's sole supporter was a Democrat; nothing indicates how the full House or Senate would have split.

industries.industry: Large universal banks (deposit-taking banks with securities underwriting affiliates)
industries.note: They would have been forced to cut ties with underwriting and distribution of securities within a year, splitting businesses built after the 1999 repeal of Glass-Steagall. Their interest in keeping the combined model ran against the bill's depositor-protection purpose.

The bill barred their officers, directors, and employees from simultaneously running member banks, and barred bank affiliations with firms principally engaged in issuing and selling securities, cutting off access to insured deposits and bank customer bases.

industries.industry: Banks selling insurance and insurance-related products
industries.note: Depository institutions would have been prohibited from the business of insurance entirely, ending a distribution channel convenient for bank customers though also a source of fee sales pressure on them.
